newsitem.title: USA: U.S. increasingly concerned about EU grain subsidies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. increasingly concerned about EU grain subsidies.

text.p: A sharp increase in European grain subsidies has heightened concern among Department of Agriculture officials, but the department's senior trade advisor said Wednesday it was not yet ready to retaliate.

"It would be fair to say the increase in the European subsidies caught our attention," said Paul Drazek, trade advisor to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. "We're very concerned about European subsidies not only on wheat, but on other products."
European nations use subsidies, cash payments to grain producers to compensate for low market prices, to promote sales of home-grown crops in overseas markets.

The European Union last week sharply hiked its wheat subsidy levels, prompting trans-Atlantic phone conversations between Drazek and EU officials in which Drazek reiterated Washington's position that subsidies are unnecessary.

Glickman will meet with EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler next month in Rome while attending the World Food Summit, and Drazek said export subsidies will figure prominently in their discussions.

After more than a year without using subsidies to push grain exports, the European Union this fall resumed its subsidy programme. European officials have denied they seek to undercut the United States, insisting the subsidies are needed to help move out Europe's bumper crop.
U.S. officials have warned Europe that they are closely monitoring the situation and will fight subsidy with subsidy if it is found Europe is indeed cutting into U.S. markets.

But Drazek said Washington officials will respond cautiously, despite a request Tuesday from the National Association of Wheat Growers to reactivate the U.S. Export Enhancement Programme (EEP), the subsidy programme for U.S. agricultural products.

"The decision to pursue an EEP initiative is a very serious matter, and any decision would have to be taken after very, very careful examination of all the factors involved," he said. "One of them clearly is what the Europeans are doing. This is not the only factor, but it's an important one."
Drazek said the Agriculture Department must consider the tight wheat supply in the United States and the potential effects of subsidies on the U.S. market.
Many grain industry analysts doubt the effectiveness of reactivating export subsidies at this time.
They claim short U.S. supplies and plentiful foreign stocks would limit how aggressively Washington could push subsidies, which could ultimately increase U.S. purchases of foreign grain.

A study by the consulting group Sparks Cos. said use of EEP this year would drive down world wheat prices, possibly sparking Canadian wheat shipments to the United States and even cutting U.S. corn exports if wheat prices fell too far.
"There are a lot of pitfalls with using the EEP at this point," said an industry official. "There are so many fish hooks in this environment, I'm not sure if it's prudent."
But the National Association of Wheat Growers urged Glickman on Tuesday to get moving.

"The administration's wait-and-see policy is not strong enough," said NAWG executive vice president Carl Schwenson. "The administration should escalate its threat against the European Union, and put the machinery in place necessary to get EEP up and running again."
